nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: During a gel manicure, the cuticle nipper nicks the client and a drop of blood hits the metal. What must happen to that implement before the next client?

options.a: Clean debris off the metal, then EPA-disinfect or autoclave it
options.b: Wipe the blood on a used towel and keep using the same nipper
options.c: Rinse the nipper in the client's soak water, then reuse it dry
options.d: Give the bloody nipper to the client as a take-home souvenir

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Blood on a multi-use metal tool is an exposure event. Remove it from service, wash off debris, then complete EPA hospital disinfection (full wet contact time) or sterilization if the board allows. Bloodied porous items such as files are discarded, not soaked.

distractorExplanations.b: A towel wipe leaves blood film on the tool and contaminates linen; it is not disinfection.
distractorExplanations.c: Pedicure soak water is not an EPA disinfectant and spreads contamination into the bowl.
distractorExplanations.d: Handing a contaminated implement to the client does not satisfy salon infection-control rules.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: A foam buffer used on a fill is scored, packed with product dust, and shows a smear of blood at the edge. What is required?

options.a: Soak it in quats overnight and return it to the bit jar
options.b: Discard it; bloodied porous buffers are not multi-use tools
options.c: Wash it with soap, air-dry, and share it on toes later
options.d: Seal it in a bag labeled for that client’s next fill visit

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Emery boards, foam buffers, and similar porous abrasives are single-use once worn, soiled, or blood-exposed. Disinfectant cannot reliably penetrate porous material. NIC-style theory treats them as discard items, not multi-use implements.

distractorExplanations.a: Quats cannot convert a bloodied porous buffer into a reusable multi-use tool.
distractorExplanations.c: Soap washing does not disinfect porous foam, and sharing it still spreads blood and fungus.
distractorExplanations.d: Salon storage of used porous files for a return visit is not an allowed disinfection method.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: A whirlpool pedicure chair just finished a soak. Before the next client sits, what must be cleaned and disinfected?

options.a: A fresh-water rinse of the visible bowl only, skipping the pipes
options.b: The jets at close of business; midday soaks can skip chemical steps
options.c: The bowl plus circulating jets, screens, and filters per the label
options.d: The chair armrests only, because biofilm cannot form in wet pipes

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Whirlpool pedicure systems grow biofilm in pipes, jets, and screens. Between clients, drain, scrub debris, then circulate EPA-registered disinfectant for the contact time, including filters the manufacturer requires. A surface rinse of the bowl leaves the infection reservoir in the plumbing.

distractorExplanations.a: Rinsing the bowl removes soil you can see but leaves biofilm in the jet circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: End-of-day deep cleaning is extra; every client still needs a full clean-and-disinfect cycle.
distractorExplanations.d: Armrest wipe-downs do not treat pipe biofilm, the main pedicure-outbreak source.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: After trimming hangnails, stainless nippers are coated with skin bits and product. What is the correct sequence before the next manicure?

options.a: Mist disinfectant on the dirty metal, then wipe it dry immediately
options.b: Soak the dirty nippers first, then try to scrub residue afterward
options.c: Wipe with a 70% alcohol pad and return them to the clean drawer
options.d: Scrub debris off, rinse, then EPA-disinfect for the contact time

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Sanitation (cleaning) removes soil; disinfection is a separate EPA kill step on a clean, nonporous surface. Debris blocks disinfectant. Metal nippers are multi-use: wash, then immerse or otherwise wet-contact for the label time. Alcohol wipe-and-go is not that process.

distractorExplanations.a: Spraying over soil and wiping dry skips cleaning and ends contact time too early.
distractorExplanations.b: Disinfecting first traps debris; soil must come off before the EPA step works.
distractorExplanations.c: A brief alcohol wipe is not hospital disinfection of a multi-use metal implement.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: The tech is about to soak, file, and massage a client's feet. Why do boards expect gloves for this pedicure?

options.a: They protect the tech from fungi/chemicals and the client from flora
options.b: They stop nipper cuts on the client but do nothing for the tech's hands
options.c: They block acetone only; intact skin already stops every foot fungus
options.d: They are optional once metal tools have been through an EPA soak

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Pedicures involve prolonged wet contact with feet, nail dust, and chemicals. Gloves are PPE: they reduce the tech's exposure to fungi, bacteria, and product, and they reduce transfer of the tech's skin flora onto the client. They do not replace tool disinfection or make cuts impossible.

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves are not cut-proof armor; their job is barrier protection for both parties, not blocking steel.
distractorExplanations.c: Fungi enter through tiny breaks; gloves protect against microbes as well as chemicals.
distractorExplanations.d: Clean tools do not protect bare hands from the client's skin, soak water, or product.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: A walk-in wants a fill. The nail plate is thick, yellow, and crumbling, and the tech suspects fungus. What is in scope?

options.a: Thin the plate aggressively and sell an in-salon antifungal polish
options.b: Stop the infected nail and refer the client to a physician
options.c: Proceed after the client signs a waiver taking all infection risk
options.d: Seal the nail in builder gel so the organism is cut off from air

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Nail technicians do not diagnose or treat infections. A suspected fungal nail is a stop-and-refer: servicing it can spread organism onto bits, files, and other clients and is outside manicurist scope. Cosmetics and waivers do not convert the service into medical care.

distractorExplanations.a: Filing and selling treatment is medical practice plus aerosolizes the fungus.
distractorExplanations.c: A waiver does not make an infected nail a legal or safe salon service.
distractorExplanations.d: Occluding a fungal nail traps moisture and hides the infection; it does not treat it.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: Foam toe separators sat between the client's toes during polish. After the pedicure, what happens to them?

options.a: Soak them in hospital disinfectant and reuse them all afternoon
options.b: Bag them at the station for the same client's next polish visit
options.c: Discard them as porous single-use items; do not disinfect to reuse
options.d: Rinse them in the whirlpool, air-dry on the hook, and restock them

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Foam toe separators are porous single-use. EPA disinfectant is for cleaned nonporous implements, not foam that absorbed soak water and skin cells. They are discarded (or given to that client to take), not returned to the drawer.

distractorExplanations.a: Hospital disinfectant does not make porous foam a multi-use implement.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping used separators for a return visit still stores a contaminated porous item.
distractorExplanations.d: Basin rinsing contaminates the bowl and never disinfects foam.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: Between clients, a tech parks wet cuticle nippers under the UV/LED gel lamp and calls that sterilization. What is true?

options.a: The lamp's wavelength is an EPA-registered hospital disinfectant for steel
options.b: Two minutes under the lamp meets typical autoclave spore-kill standards
options.c: Curing light replaces cleaning because heat dries leftover skin debris
options.d: The lamp cures gel; it does not replace EPA disinfection of metal tools

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: UV/LED units polymerize gel. They are not sterilizers and not EPA hospital disinfectants. Multi-use metal tools still need debris removed, then wet disinfection or true sterilization (e.g., autoclave where allowed). Dry heat from a lamp is not that step.

distractorExplanations.a: Gel lamps are not labeled EPA hospital disinfectants for implements.
distractorExplanations.b: Sterilization requires a validated autoclave cycle, not a manicure lamp.
distractorExplanations.c: Drying debris does not clean or disinfect; soil still blocks any later chemical.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: The tech removes gloves after a pedicure and walks to the polish wall. When is soap-and-water handwashing still required?

options.a: Before and after each client, and again right after gloves come off
options.b: Only before the first soak; gloves fully replace washing afterward
options.c: At clock-in and after lunch, skipping the steps between ticketed clients
options.d: Only when product or soak water is obvious on the palms

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Hands are washed before and after every client. Gloves are not a substitute: they leak and the removal step contaminates skin. OSHA-style bloodborne practice also expects washing after glove removal, not only when soil is visible.

distractorExplanations.b: Gloves tear and come off dirty; washing after removal is still required.
distractorExplanations.c: Shift and meal washing does not replace per-client and post-glove washing.
distractorExplanations.d: Pathogens are not always visible; waiting for obvious soil is too late.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: A sanding band snapped, a callus blade was used, and a cotton round is blood-spotted. What needs a covered sharps or blood-waste plan?

options.a: Unopened emery boards still in the original sleeve on the cart
options.b: Used blades, e-file bands, and bloodied single-use cotton or gauze
options.c: Empty gel bottles and cardboard product boxes from today's order
options.d: Clean folded towels and unused cotton rounds in the closed cabinet

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: OSHA bloodborne rules and board sanitation outlines require puncture-resistant or covered disposal for contaminated sharps and blood-soaked disposables. Clean unused stock and ordinary packaging are not that waste stream.

distractorExplanations.a: Factory-sealed files have not contacted blood or skin; they are not sharps waste.
distractorExplanations.c: Empty retail packaging is ordinary trash or recycling, not bloodborne waste.
distractorExplanations.d: Unused linens and cotton are clean inventory, not an exposure discard.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: After an acrylic fill, a multi-use carbide bit is caked with dust. How is it processed before the next client?

options.a: Wipe it with acetone and mount it for the next fill immediately
options.b: Drop it in disinfectant first, then brush product off the flutes
options.c: Brush and wash debris off, then EPA-disinfect or sterilize the metal
options.d: Rinse under tap water, air-dry on a towel, and return it to the case

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Carbide bits contact the nail plate and are multi-use only after cleaning then disinfection or sterilization. Product dust must be brushed and washed off first so EPA solution contacts metal. Acetone and water are not hospital disinfectants.

distractorExplanations.a: Acetone removes acrylic residue but is not an EPA-registered disinfectant.
distractorExplanations.b: Soaking a dirty bit first lets debris shield microbes from the chemical.
distractorExplanations.d: A water rinse is sanitation at best; it does not complete disinfection.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: The immersion jar of EPA hospital disinfectant is cloudy and full of skin specks. What should the tech do?

options.a: Top it off with tap water so the tools stay fully covered
options.b: Use the cloudy mix as a skin antiseptic before cuticle work
options.c: Pour it into the whirlpool as a 'stronger' pedicure disinfectant
options.d: Discard it, wash the jar, and remix to the EPA label dilution

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Cloudy, debris-loaded disinfectant is spent and contaminated. Change it, wash the container, and remake to the EPA label concentration and date. Diluting, putting it on skin, or dumping it into a pedicure system misuses the product.

distractorExplanations.a: Adding water under-dilutes the EPA mix and leaves organic load in the jar.
distractorExplanations.b: Implement disinfectant is not a leave-on antiseptic for living skin.
distractorExplanations.c: Spent jar solution is not a substitute for labeled pedicure-basin disinfectant.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: While prepping for a pedicure, the tech sees a rough, cauliflower-like wart on the client's heel. What is the correct action?

options.a: Do not work over the lesion; stop that area and refer out
options.b: Cover the wart with a sticky bandage and continue the soak
options.c: Buff the growth down with a fine grit so polish lies flat
options.d: Book the client last, service the wart, then disinfect tools

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Plantar warts are contagious viral lesions. Manicurists do not treat them. Working over the site, filing it, or 'going last' still spreads virus onto tools, linens, and basins. Skip the lesion and refer to a physician or podiatrist.

distractorExplanations.b: A bandage does not make a viral wart safe to soak, file, or massage over.
distractorExplanations.c: Buffing a wart aerosolizes virus and is medical treatment, not nail care.
distractorExplanations.d: End-of-day scheduling does not authorize servicing an infectious lesion.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: The salon stacks one terry cloth for several afternoon pedicures if it 'looks dry.' Why does each client still need a freshly laundered towel?

options.a: Mostly to wipe EPA residue off the basin before the next soak
options.b: To stop sharing skin cells, sweat, and fungal spores between feet
options.c: So the whirlpool can skip jet disinfection when the towel is clean
options.d: Dry used towels may go back on the open shelf without laundry

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Linens that touched feet are single-client. Even a dry towel carries skin squames and fungal spores. Boards require a clean towel per person and proper laundry; towels are not a substitute for basin disinfection.

distractorExplanations.a: Residue control is rinsing the bowl; fresh towels exist to block cross-infection.
distractorExplanations.c: A clean towel never replaces circulating EPA disinfection of whirlpool plumbing.
distractorExplanations.d: Dryness is not sanitation; used towels must be laundered before any reuse.

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.prompt: A pipe-less pedicure tub has no whirlpool jets. After draining the soak, what is still required before the next client?

options.a: Leave standing soak water in the tub because there are no pipes
options.b: Wipe the basin dry with yesterday's towel and skip chemicals
options.c: Wash off debris, then EPA-disinfect the basin for full contact time
options.d: Spray acetone around the tub and count that as hospital disinfection

nail-technician-state-readiness-check-in.explanation: Pipe-less and liner-style tubs still contact feet, skin cells, and soak product. Between clients they are cleaned of debris and wet-disinfected with an EPA-registered product for the labeled time. No jets does not mean no disinfection; acetone is not a hospital disinfectant.

distractorExplanations.a: Standing used soak water is contamination, not a disinfection step.
distractorExplanations.b: A dry wipe, especially with a used towel, does not meet EPA contact time.
distractorExplanations.d: Acetone is a solvent for product, not an EPA hospital disinfectant for basins.
